qa_source.question: distinguish between shipowner’s lien & maritime lien
reference_answers: A Shipowner 's Lien is a possessory lien which is the major difference between it and other maritime liens. It may entitle the shipowner to retain the cargoes as security for the payment of a debt. However , some authorities state that there is no difference between shipowner 's lien and maritime lien.

used_documents.title: Maritime lien
used_documents.text: A Shipowner 's Lien is a possessory lien which is the major difference between it and other maritime liens . The right to this lien can be applied only on the goods which are delivering by the shipowner when the shipper is the contractual party . It may entitle the shipowner to retain the cargoes as security for the payment of a debt . The contractual shipowner 's lien is currently found in all contracts for carriage of goods by sea nowadays , and may be claimed if the shippers fail to pay the due on time . However , some authorities state that there is no difference between shipowner 's lien and maritime lien .

For instance , in the United States , a federal tax lien , which is a non-maritime lien , is subordinate to every lien for supplies , fuel , repairs , etc. , which are all maritime liens .

used_documents.title: Maritime lien
used_documents.text: It is a proprietary lien where interest is about the property . It should be understood that `` res '' may be the vessel ( including its appurtenances and equipment ) , the cargo , the freight or even the proceeds of sale . The rights include jus in re ( right on the property ) and jus in rem ( right against the property ) . The doctrine of maritime lien is that a ship will be treated as a wrongdoer , not the owner , that the loss , damage or harm is caused by the maritime property , itself , and it has to make good for the loss . The attachment of maritime lien will start when the cause of action arises and will not be eliminated even by change of ownership in a good faith purchase .

A.answer: The shipowner's lien is a possessory lien that applies only to goods delivered by the shipowner when the shipper is the contractual party. It allows the shipowner to retain the cargoes as security for the payment of a debt. Maritime liens, on the other hand, are privileged claims upon sea-connected property such as a ship, for services rendered to, or injuries caused by that property. Maritime liens are superior to non-maritime liens and can be discharged or eliminated through various means. [771847086_4176-4795] [771847086_1188-1478] [771847086_1479-2172]

annotation.essential_points: Explain that a shipowner's lien is possessory and permits retaining cargo as debt security, while a maritime lien is a privileged claim against maritime property.
annotation.reason: The answer explains the central distinction between possessory cargo retention and a privileged claim against maritime property. evidence.quote: A Shipowner 's Lien is a possessory lien which is the major difference between it and other maritime liens . The right to this lien can be applied only on the goods which are delivering by the shipowner when the shipper is the contractual party . It may entitle the shipowner to retain the cargoes as security for the payment of a debt . The contractual shipowner 's lien is currently found in all contracts for carriage of goods by sea nowadays , and may be claimed if the shippers fail to pay the due on time . However , some authorities state that there is no difference between shipowner 's lien and maritime lien .

Two significant differences between maritime liens , which only exist in admiralty law , and the right to keep that exist in general civil law are ( 1 ) that in general civil law , `` Prior in time is prior in right '' , i.e. , the rights of the lienholder with the earliest lien are superior to those of later lienholders , whereas in maritime law the rights of the most recent lienholder are superior , and ( 2 ) all maritime liens are superior to all non-maritime liens . For instance , in the United States , a federal tax lien , which is a non-maritime lien , is subordinate to every lien for supplies , fuel , repairs , etc. , which are all maritime liens .

Although the maritime lien is attached to the maritime property whoever the shipowner is , it is possible to discharge or eliminate the lien by several ways . They include payment of the claims , waiver , laches , foreclosure , and sale or destruction of the res .

In admiralty law , a maritime lien is a privileged claim upon sea - connected property , such as a ship , for services rendered to , or the injuries caused by that property . In common law , a lien is the right of the creditor to retain the properties of his debtor until the debt is paid .

B.answer: A shipowner's lien is a possessory lien applied only on goods delivered by the shipowner when the shipper is the contractual party, allowing retention of cargoes for debt payment [4176-4795]. Conversely, a maritime lien is a privileged claim upon sea-connected property, such as a ship, for services rendered or injuries caused by that property [1188-1478]. While a shipowner's lien is possessory, a maritime lien is a proprietary lien where interest is about the property itself [1479-2172]. Furthermore, all maritime liens are superior to non-maritime liens [2173-2836], and they can be discharged or eliminated through means such as payment, waiver, laches, foreclosure, or sale of the res [6067-6331].

evidence.quote: A Shipowner 's Lien is a possessory lien which is the major difference between it and other maritime liens . The right to this lien can be applied only on the goods which are delivering by the shipowner when the shipper is the contractual party . It may entitle the shipowner to retain the cargoes as security for the payment of a debt . The contractual shipowner 's lien is currently found in all contracts for carriage of goods by sea nowadays , and may be claimed if the shippers fail to pay the due on time . However , some authorities state that there is no difference between shipowner 's lien and maritime lien .

Two significant differences between maritime liens , which only exist in admiralty law , and the right to keep that exist in general civil law are ( 1 ) that in general civil law , `` Prior in time is prior in right '' , i.e. , the rights of the lienholder with the earliest lien are superior to those of later lienholders , whereas in maritime law the rights of the most recent lienholder are superior , and ( 2 ) all maritime liens are superior to all non-maritime liens . For instance , in the United States , a federal tax lien , which is a non-maritime lien , is subordinate to every lien for supplies , fuel , repairs , etc. , which are all maritime liens .

Although the maritime lien is attached to the maritime property whoever the shipowner is , it is possible to discharge or eliminate the lien by several ways . They include payment of the claims , waiver , laches , foreclosure , and sale or destruction of the res .

In admiralty law , a maritime lien is a privileged claim upon sea - connected property , such as a ship , for services rendered to , or the injuries caused by that property . In common law , a lien is the right of the creditor to retain the properties of his debtor until the debt is paid .

It is a proprietary lien where interest is about the property . It should be understood that `` res '' may be the vessel ( including its appurtenances and equipment ) , the cargo , the freight or even the proceeds of sale . The rights include jus in re ( right on the property ) and jus in rem ( right against the property ) . The doctrine of maritime lien is that a ship will be treated as a wrongdoer , not the owner , that the loss , damage or harm is caused by the maritime property , itself , and it has to make good for the loss . The attachment of maritime lien will start when the cause of action arises and will not be eliminated even by change of ownership in a good faith purchase .
